newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian local polls may be held in June -- OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian local polls may be held in June -- OSCE.

text.p: The U.S. envoy overseeing Bosnian elections said on Saturday that the country's first peacetime local polls would probably be held in June 1997.
"My recommendation is June," said Ambassador Robert Frowick, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission in Bosnia.
"It gives us many months yet to prepare," Frowick told reporters.
The local polls, which were initially supposed to have coincided with national elections in September, have been plagued by controversy and were postponed twice.
Former warring factions view the municipal vote as a battle for control of disputed territory which they fought over during the 1992-1995 Bosnian conflict.
Frowick said setting the ballot for June would give the OSCE mission time to strengthen its supervision of voter registration both in Bosnia and abroad.
But he said delaying the municipal polls later in 1997 could open the way to scrapping international monitoring altogether.
Diplomats said the OSCE would probably hold the local elections over two days and provide one international monitor at each of the 2,500 polling stations.
Reports that Bosnian Serb authorities were manipulating the registration of Serb refugees led the OSCE to postpone the municipal elections in the autumn.
Leaders of Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic have since been at odds over rules governing the registration of refugees, whose votes will be crucial to the election outcome.
The parties have to agree electoral rules by January 31.
Frowick acknowleged the municipal polls were a subject of sharp disagreement but said the Dayton peace agreement obliged both sides to reach a compromise.

The Dayton accords signed a year ago say voters are expected to vote in districts where they lived before the war but also allow for refugees and displaced people to apply to cast their ballots elsewhere.
"The point of departure must be the Dayton agreement. All sides have got to realise that was a compromise," Frowick said.

Serb authorities, accused of trying to stack the odds in their favour, registered large numbers of refugees earlier this year under a provision which allowed them to vote in towns where they "intended" to live.
The OSCE has decided to conduct a new, modified registration for the municipal polls.

OSCE officials have discussed proposals with Serb leaders which would require refugees to meet certain criteria to win the right to vote where they "intend" to live, proving they had relatives or a job offer in the district.
Voters chose a national inter-ethnic parliament and a collective three-member presidency in general elections held in September in Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.
The general elections, in which Moslem, Serb and Croat nationalist parties prevailed, went off without any serious violence and were deemed a success by major powers.
But opposition parties said they never had a chance because the media were strictly controlled by the ruling nationalist parties and voters were coerced by authorities.
